title: Wideband microwave resonator for NV center vector magnetometry
authors: S. V. Bolshedvorskii, E. A. Koreshin, V. V. Soshenko, I. S. Cojocaru, S. M. Drofa, P. G. Vilyuzhanina, N. I. Salangin, A. M. Kozodaev, A. Chernyavskiy, A. N. Smolyaninov, P. V. Kapitanova, S. Ya. Kilin, A. V. Akimov
abstract: The nitrogen-vacancy (NV) color center in diamond has found applications in magnetometry across various geometrical scales. In particular, vector magnetometry using hand-held devices with low power consumption is of interest for mobile and geological applications. However, such a device requires efficient driving of the four different orientations of the NV center, thus placing demands on a broadband microwave resonator that provides a uniform and highly insensitive microwave magnetic field at the resonance frequencies of the NV centers. Here, we propose a unique planar resonator design that enables efficient driving of all four orientations of NV color centers over a 100 MHz range with only 0.5 W of microwave input power and 250 mW of laser power, allowing vector magnetic field measurements. Using the planar resonator to drive NV centers in diamond, a compact vector magnetometer was fabricated and experimentally studied. The sensitivity of the device is about \[{1.2\text{ nT}}/{\sqrt{\text{Hz}}}\;\]. While this is not a record sensitivity for diamond-based magnetometers, this device occupies its own niche as a compact hand-held magnetometer.
summary: This paper presents the design and experimental realization of a compact, hand-held vector magnetometer based on NV centers in diamond. The key innovation is a planar microwave resonator that efficiently drives the multiple resonance orientations required for full vector measurement over a wide frequency band. The resulting device achieves a sensitivity of 1.2 nT/sqrt(Hz), making it a practical tool for mobile magnetic sensing applications.
main_problem: The goal is to develop a compact, hand-held vector magnetometer using Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond that can efficiently measure the magnetic field vector across multiple orientations.
main_result: The authors successfully fabricated and tested a planar microwave resonator design that enables broadband, uniform driving of the NV centers, achieving a device sensitivity of about 1.2 nT/sqrt(Hz).
method: The study involves designing and optimizing a planar microwave resonator topology (specifically Topology 3) to generate a uniform, broadband microwave magnetic field, which is then used to measure the NV center's spin resonance frequencies via ODMR spectroscopy.
model_or_system: The physical system is the NV color center in diamond, whose spin Hamiltonian is analyzed. The measurement relies on the vector magnetometry protocol, which interrogates four distinct ODMR peaks corresponding to different crystallographic orientations.
key_observables: Magnetic field vector components ($\mathbf{B}$), resonance frequencies ($f_i$), and the final measured sensitivity ($1.2 	ext{ nT}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$).
important_parameters: 100 MHz bandwidth, 0.5 W microwave input power, and the planar resonator's low Q-factor design.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the planar resonator can provide a sufficiently uniform and broadband microwave field to excite all necessary NV orientations simultaneously for vector measurement.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of three resonator topologies, showing simulated reflection coefficients, magnetic field amplitudes, and uniformity histograms, culminating in the selection of the best performing planar design.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the need for a broadband resonator for vector magnetometry, through simulating and comparing multiple resonator topologies, to fabricating the optimal planar design and finally demonstrating the measurement protocol and sensitivity.
why_interesting: This work directly applies principles of quantum sensing using solid-state defects (NV centers) and requires detailed knowledge of microwave engineering and quantum Hamiltonian analysis, making it highly relevant to AMO physics.
